issues.legal_issue: An allottee who accepts land on an as-is-where-is basis under a lease placing responsibility for its own infrastructure on the allottee has no contractual right to require the lessor to provide an access road.
material_facts: The company accepted the land under a lease expressly made on an as-is-where-is basis and without protest.
The lease placed responsibility on the company to construct and maintain an approach road from the public or corporation road to its premises.
The lease contemplated charges if the lessor chose to provide a link road, but did not require the lessor to do so.
The company sought a direction in writ proceedings requiring the lessor to provide an access road.
issues.conclusion: The lessor had no obligation to provide the access road, and the company had no legal right to obtain a writ compelling it to do so.
issues.legal_principle: Contractual terms are interpreted according to their language and cannot be rewritten to impose an obligation the parties did not agree to. Acceptance of land on an as-is-where-is basis precludes a later claim to amenities not promised. A writ of mandamus requires an existing legal right and corresponding legal duty. The Court relied on United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Harchand Rai Chandan Lal, AIR 2004 SC 4794; Polymat India P. Ltd. v. National Insurance Co. Ltd., AIR 2005 SC 286; Punjab Urban Planning & Development Authority v. Raghu Nath Gupta, (2012) 8 SCC 197; Bareilly Development Authority v. Ajay Pal Singh, AIR 1989 SC 1076; and State of U.P. v. Bridge & Roof Co. (India) Ltd., AIR 1996 SC 3515.

predicates.writ_seeks_access_road: The allottee asked a court in writ proceedings to require the lessor to provide an access road.
predicates.land_accepted_as_is_where_is: The allottee accepted the land on an as-is-where-is basis.
predicates.lease_places_road_responsibility_on_allo: The lease assigns responsibility for constructing the approach road to the allottee.

issues.definition: When an allottee seeks an access road through writ proceedings after accepting land as-is-where-is under a lease that assigns road construction to the allottee, the lessor has no duty to provide the road.

issues.legal_issue: A deeming provision that treats an allottee as a direct lessee of the State for the purpose of further subletting does not thereby divest the original development body of its title or interest in the land.
material_facts: The State transferred acquired land to the development body after receiving consideration, and the development body later leased part of it to the company.
An amendment enabled the company to grant further subleases and applied relevant rules to it as if the land had been let to it by the State.
The amendment was introduced to facilitate further subletting, and did not expressly transfer the development body's title or interest in the land.
The High Court treated the deeming language as making the State the lessor and removing the development body's authority over the land.
issues.conclusion: The deeming language applied only to facilitate further subletting and did not remove the development body's title or rights in the land.
issues.legal_principle: A legal fiction must be given effect for the purpose for which it was created, including necessary consequences, but must not be extended beyond that purpose. “Mutatis mutandis” imports necessary changes in points of detail without changing the essential nature of what is adapted. The Court relied on Rule 11-A of the Rajasthan Land Revenue (Industrial Area Allotment) Rules, 1959, as amended; M/s. Ashok Service Centre v. State of Orissa, AIR 1983 SC 394; Prahlad Sharma v. State of U.P., (2004) 4 SCC 113; East End Dwelling Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council, 1952 AC 109; and Industrial Supplies Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1980 SC 1858.

predicates.dispute_concerns_scope_of_subleasing_fic: The dispute concerns whether a legal deeming provision for further subletting changes the original development body's rights in the land.
predicates.land_was_transferred_to_development_body: The State transferred the land to a development body after receiving consideration.
predicates.deeming_language_enables_further_sublett: A legal provision treats the allottee as a direct lessee for the purpose of allowing further subletting.

issues.definition: If a dispute concerns a subletting deeming provision and the land was transferred to a development body for consideration, language enabling further subletting does not divest that body's title.

issues.legal_issue: An allotment may be cancelled when the allottee substantially fails to complete the required development within the agreed period and does not obtain a valid extension after notice of the breach.
material_facts: The lease required completion of construction and commencement of production within the stipulated period.
At the end of that period, only about ten percent of the total construction had been completed.
The company did not make a proper application for an extension specifying the additional time sought and satisfying the applicable requirements.
The development body issued a show-cause notice and then cancelled the allotment under the applicable land-disposal rules and lease terms.
issues.conclusion: The cancellation was valid, and the order cancelling the company's allotment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The allottee was bound by the lease's completion requirements, and cancellation could be made for breach after a show-cause notice under Rule 24 of the Rajasthan State Industrial & Investment Corporation Limited (Disposal of Land) Rules, 1979, read with the lease terms. The Court also relied on the lease provisions requiring timely construction and production and permitting re-entry upon breach.

rule.if: industrial_land_lease_cancellation and construction_was_substantially_incomplete_at_deadline and no_valid_extension_was_obtained and show_cause_notice_was_given

predicates.industrial_land_lease_cancellation: The proceeding concerns cancellation of an industrial land allotment for breach of its lease conditions.
predicates.construction_was_substantially_incomplet: The allottee had completed only a small part of the required construction by the agreed deadline.
predicates.no_valid_extension_was_obtained: The allottee had not obtained a valid extension of the time for completion.
predicates.show_cause_notice_was_given: The authority gave the allottee notice to show cause before cancelling the allotment.

issues.definition: In an industrial land cancellation proceeding, substantial non-completion by the deadline, absence of a valid extension, and prior show-cause notice support a valid cancellation.

issues.legal_issue: A writ petition should not be used to resolve a contractual dispute or challenge a contractual allotment decision where the allottee has available statutory or contractual remedies.
material_facts: The company challenged the cancellation of its land allotment by writ petition.
The dispute concerned compliance with the lease and the authority's contractual and rule-based power to cancel the allotment.
The rules provided for review and appeal, and the lease contained an arbitration clause.
The company did not use those remedies before filing its writ petition.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition, and the company should have pursued the available alternative remedies.
issues.legal_principle: Contractual disputes and disputes over interpretation or implementation of contract terms ordinarily cannot be resolved through a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. A claimant should resort to available statutory or contractual remedies; the Court relied on Article 226, Rule 24(aa) and Rule 24(bb)(ii) of the Rajasthan State Industrial & Investment Corporation Limited (Disposal of Land) Rules, 1979, the lease's arbitration clause, Bareilly Development Authority v. Ajay Pal Singh, AIR 1989 SC 1076; State of U.P. v. Bridge & Roof Co. (India) Ltd., AIR 1996 SC 3515; and Kerala State Electricity Board v. Kurien E. Kalathil, AIR 2000 SC 2573.

predicates.writ_challenges_contractual_allotment_ac: The proceeding is a writ petition challenging an action concerning a contractual land allotment.
predicates.contractual_terms_are_in_dispute: The dispute turns on the interpretation or performance of the allotment's contractual terms.
predicates.effective_alternative_remedies_are_avail: The claimant has available statutory or contractual procedures for review, appeal, or resolution of the dispute.

issues.definition: A writ challenging a contractual allotment action should not be entertained when the dispute concerns contract terms and effective alternative remedies are available.
